title: The Rock Who Loved Paperwork
markdown:
The Grand Interstellar Port of Zephyr Prime was a swirling, humming nexus where wormholes spat out travelers from every corner of existence. Shimmering energy. Ozone mixed with exotic spice. A million engines changing their minds. At the heart of it stood Neve Sarin, a whiz with a datapad and a champion of the professional sigh. Greet every incoming soul. Check the documents. Make sure no contraband, no space-slugs, and certainly no rogue nebulae hitched a ride. Most days were scan, holographic stamp, polite nod. Glorgons with three blinking eyes. Fuzzy Xylosians who smelled faintly of cinnamon. Stoic automatons who communicated solely through interpretive dance. Neve did it well and harbored, in the cracks, a longing for uncharted nebulae and lost civilizations rather than transit forms for people in glow-in-the-dark boots and the occasional sentient fungus. It felt like a tedious corner of the universe.

Then, one Tuesday, a peculiar passenger waddled up. A very nice, very smooth grey rock, about the size of a grapefruit, with a faint shimmer as if a thousand stellar winds had polished it. No antennae. No limbs. Just rock. A crack near the top opened and a voice, surprisingly polite and a touch squeaky, asked to file arrival documentation.

Neve blinked. The datapad slipped. Sir? Madam? Rock? Geological specimens were scanned for valuable minerals or planetary-core fragments.

The rock, which Neve would learn was Mr. Pebble, vibrated, a subtle hum on the smooth surface. Indeed. A tourist. A seasoned interplanetary explorer. And as a responsible traveler, it insisted on completing the Universal Transit Declaration, Form 7G, Sub-section Delta, the Inter-dimensional Visitors’ Intent Survey, Form 9, and the Xenological Personal Effects Inventory, Form 12B.

Therefore Neve rummaged the holographic display, the digital equivalent of a mountain of paper. Form 7G was for multi-dimensional beings who phased through solid matter and whose home dimensions would not sit still. Form 9 was for those whose sole purpose was contemplation of cosmic dust, a surprisingly common claim. Form 12B was for sentient amoebas importing extra sludge. The slime samples, Neve admitted, were usually interesting.

Mr. Pebble remained steadfast. Precisely. All completed. Meticulously. Thoroughness. No unsanctioned stellar dust bunnies, no unregistered teleportation devices, no anything unaccounted for. Luggage: unique atmospheric samples and a particularly vibrant bioluminescent moss.

Neve, dry even when faced with a talking rock who held a doctorate in bureaucracy, chuckled. Unique traveler. Most aliens tried to skip forms by disguising themselves as inanimate objects. Mr. Pebble seemed to be collecting them.

Efficiency, it chirped, a faint shimmer of approval. The universe ran on order. A well-filed form was the first step to universal peace. It prevented misunderstandings, clarified intentions, and, most importantly, kept anyone from bringing a carnivorous plant that ate paperwork into the port. Now, about Annex C of the Personal Effects Inventory, detailing the nutritional value of the companion lichen.

Hours ticked. The manageable queue stretched like a cosmic serpent. Passengers with tentacles or flashing lights or the capacity to spontaneously combust from impatience grumbled and fidgeted. Gorlak, a particularly large green alien with what looked like six elbows, a notorious smuggler of rare and usually very smelly fruit, saw the delay as a golden chance. He nudged Neve, gruff, pointing. Ridiculous. Just a rock. His Lumina-berries were time-sensitive. They ripened for precisely one standard cycle after leaving home. After that, mush.

But Neve, strangely fascinated by the unwavering protocol, and quite fond of proving Gorlak wrong, kept sorting the perfectly filled forms. Emotional state: calmly observant. Primary travel objective: experiential data acquisition, with a secondary focus on local culinary delights. A tiny dandelion seed from a previous journey, encased in a miniature transparent sphere, labeled non-contaminant, natural souvenir, Exhibit A. Origin: Terra, Sector 7, Quadrant Gamma. Quiet rebellion against a man who thought berries outranked rules.

The conflict was not only Neve versus a mounting port. It was order and chaos in a booth: Mr. Pebble and Gorlak. The other travelers, impatient, watched with bewilderment and grudging admiration. A collective sigh, larger than Neve’s usual, swept the waiting area. Neve began to suspect the rock was not merely a peculiar tourist with a hobby. There was purpose in the meticulousness, a lesson aimed especially at people who thought they could walk around the system.

The last form was the most complex, a multi-page snare for smugglers of exotic diseases and rogue sentient microbes: non-standard bio-signatures. Mr. Pebble had filled it with a single elegant sentence in impossibly neat tiny script. Its purpose was to demonstrate that even the smallest, seemingly insignificant entity could uphold the grandest universal principles through diligent protocol, fostering trust and order in the vast beautiful chaos, and preventing the proliferation of subpar, overripe Lumina-berries.

Neve looked at the rock. At the holographic pyramid of forms. At Gorlak, now sheepish, berries beginning to droop. At the patient line, which had become an audience. Annoyance in the port had thinned into a strange quiet admiration. Then it clicked. Not just a tourist. An ambassador of doing the thing properly, and the checkmate to Gorlak’s schemes.

You’ve caused a stir, Neve said, a genuine smile. A considerable one. And you’ve shown everyone here, including Gorlak, that even in the chaos of intergalactic travel there is value in doing it right. Not just a rock. A lesson in dedication.

Mr. Pebble glowed a little warmer. The intention had been to inspire. And perhaps to secure a booking at the Galactic Gastronomy Festival. Nebula Noodle Soups. Quasar Quiches. The legendary Zero-G Soufflé. The comprehensive application for Most Enthusiastic Visitor should arrive shortly.

Neve laughed, a sound that got above the engines. Thanks to the perfect paperwork and the defense of principle, the festival could be arranged. And maybe a tutorial on Sub-section Delta, which had always been a mystery. And perhaps Gorlak could learn patience while his berries considered a second career as jam.

Mr. Pebble, the rock who loved forms, became an accidental celebrity, a symbol of bureaucratic excellence and a surprising bane to smugglers. Travelers from all over the sector stopped at Neve’s booth hoping for a glimpse of the organized tourist. Neve Sarin, who had dreamed of adventure, found it at her own desk: a rock, a queue, Gorlak muttering over jam, and the discovery that the most exciting thing in the port that Tuesday had refused to skip a single annex. She booked the festival. She learned Sub-section Delta. She kept the sigh, because some tools are worth keeping, and watched the next wormhole open with something like appetite.
